triples.relationship: prophetic messages directed to Nineveh
triples.rationale: Nahum identifies his book as an oracle concerning Nineveh. Jonah receives the Lord's command to go to that named city and proclaim because its wickedness has come before Him. Both explicitly identify Nineveh as the destination of prophetic address.
triples.source_text: An oracle concerning Nineveh; the book of the vision of Nahum the Elkoshite.

target_units.text: The word of the Lord came to Jonah, the son of Amittai, saying:
“Rise and go to Nineveh, the great city, and proclaim in it, for the outcry of its wickedness has come up to Me.”

triples.relationship: the Lord explicitly described as jealous
triples.rationale: Nahum calls the Lord a jealous and avenging God. Exodus likewise names Him Jealous and calls Him a jealous God when forbidding worship of another god. The shared description is explicit, while Nahum emphasizes vengeance upon adversaries.
triples.source_text: The Lord is a jealous and avenging God, the Lord avenging with fury, the Lord avenging Himself on His adversaries, and He Himself removes His enemies.

target_units.text: You shall not bow down to another god, for the Lord God, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God.

triples.relationship: vengeance and judgment belonging to the Lord
triples.rationale: Nahum presents the Lord avenging Himself upon adversaries and removing enemies. Deuteronomy likewise places repayment in His day of vengeance and announces His judgment, while also speaking of concern for His weakened servants.
triples.source_text: The Lord is a jealous and avenging God, the Lord avenging with fury, the Lord avenging Himself on His adversaries, and He Himself removes His enemies.

target_units.text: In the day of vengeance I will repay, in the season when their foot shall slip; for the day of their destruction is near, and the things prepared for you are at hand.
For the Lord shall judge His people, and be moved concerning His servants; for He saw them weakened, and failing under assault, and exhausted.

triples.relationship: patience joined to the refusal to acquit guilt
triples.rationale: Nahum places the Lord's patience beside the declaration that He certainly will not acquit. Exodus likewise describes Him as slow to anger and merciful while saying that He does not cleanse the guilty. Neither passage makes patience an absence of judgment.
triples.source_text: The Lord is patient, and His strength is great; the Lord certainly will not acquit. His way is in consummation and shaking; clouds are the dust of His feet.

target_units.text: The Lord passed before him and proclaimed, “The Lord God, compassionate and merciful, slow to anger, abundant in mercy and true,

preserving righteousness and showing mercy to thousands, taking away lawlessness, injustice, and sins, yet not cleansing the guilty, bringing the fathers’ lawlessness upon children and children’s children to the third and fourth generation.”

triples.relationship: the Lord's threat dries seas and rivers
triples.rationale: Nahum says the Lord threatens the sea and dries it, making rivers desolate. Isaiah likewise describes His threat making the sea desolate and turning rivers to deserts. Both expressly connect desiccated waters with His power.
triples.source_text: He threatens the sea and dries it up, and makes all the rivers desolate. Bashan and Carmel have dwindled, and Lebanon’s flowering things have failed.

target_units.text: Why did I come when no person was there, call when no one obeyed? Is My hand not strong enough to rescue? Am I not able to deliver? Behold, by My threat I will make the sea desolate and turn rivers to deserts; their fish will dry up for lack of water and die in thirst.

triples.relationship: the Lord makes the sea dry
triples.rationale: Nahum describes the Lord drying the sea. Exodus narrates a particular occasion when He drives the sea back and makes it dry so that Israel can pass through. The historical scene supplies an explicit example of power over the sea, without identifying it as Nahum's only referent.
triples.source_text: He threatens the sea and dries it up, and makes all the rivers desolate. Bashan and Carmel have dwindled, and Lebanon’s flowering things have failed.

target_units.text: Moses stretched out his hand over the sea. The Lord drove the sea back with a violent south wind all night and made the sea dry. The water was split.
The sons of Israel entered the midst of the sea on dry ground, and the water was a wall for them on the right and a wall on the left.

triples.relationship: mountains and earth shaken before the Lord
triples.rationale: Nahum describes mountains and hills shaken and the earth recoiling before the Lord. The psalm likewise depicts mountains and hills moving and expressly says the earth was shaken before Him. The images concern creation's response to His presence.
triples.source_text: Mountains shook before Him and hills were shaken; the whole earth recoiled before Him, and all who dwell in it.

target_units.text: The mountains skipped like rams, and the hills like lambs of sheep.
What is it with you, sea, that you fled, and with you, Jordan, that you withdrew backward?
Mountains, that you skipped like rams, and hills, like lambs of sheep?
Before the Lord the earth was shaken, before the God of Jacob,

triples.relationship: the question of standing before divine appearance and melting imagery
triples.rationale: Nahum asks who can stand before the Lord's anger and says His fury melts rulers. Malachi likewise asks who will stand at the coming appearance and describes smelting and melting the sons of Levi. The shared question and melting imagery have different subjects and purposes in their respective contexts.
triples.source_text: Who will stand before His anger? Who will resist His furious wrath? His fury melts rulers, and rocks were crushed before Him.

target_units.text: And who will endure the day of his entrance? Or who will stand at his appearance? For he enters like a smelting fire and like launderers’ herb.

He will sit, smelting and purifying as with silver and gold. He will cleanse the sons of Levi and melt them like gold and silver, and they will be those who bring a sacrifice to the Lord in righteousness.

triples.relationship: the Lord's goodness to those who wait for Him
triples.rationale: Nahum says the Lord is good to those waiting for Him in affliction. Lamentations likewise explicitly calls Him good to those who wait for Him and describes enduring quietly for His salvation. The connection preserves Nahum's waiting language rather than importing a stronghold image.
triples.source_text: The Lord is good to those who wait for Him in a day of affliction, and He knows those who revere Him.

target_units.text: The Lord is good to those who wait for Him, to the soul that will seek Him as good
and will endure and be quiet for the Lord’s salvation.

triples.relationship: an overwhelming advance represented by powerful waters
triples.rationale: Nahum pictures an advancing flood making an end of opponents. Isaiah likewise pictures strong river water advancing over walls and filling the country, explicitly identifying its force with the Assyrian king. The image is shared, while Assyria's role and the people threatened differ.
triples.source_text: With an advancing flood He will make a complete end of those who rise up, and darkness will pursue His enemies.

target_units.text: therefore, behold, the Lord brings up against you the river’s strong and abundant water—the king of the Assyrians and his glory. He will ascend every ravine of yours and walk over every wall of yours,
and he will remove from Judea a person able to lift a head or someone strong enough to accomplish anything. His encampment will fill the breadth of your country. God is with us.”

triples.relationship: counsel opposed to God cannot endure
triples.rationale: Nahum asks what is devised against the Lord before announcing His complete end. Isaiah likewise says that the Lord will scatter devised counsel and that the spoken word will not endure. The connection concerns failed opposition, not a claim that Isaiah repeats Nahum's statement about vengeance twice.
triples.source_text: What do you devise against the Lord? He will make a complete end; He will not exact vengeance twice upon the same thing in affliction.

target_units.text: Whatever counsel you devise, the Lord will scatter; whatever word you speak will certainly not endure for you, because the Lord God is with us.

triples.relationship: destructive burning pictured through vegetation
triples.rationale: Nahum compares consumption with an entwining thorn-vine and dry stubble. Isaiah describes burning against glory and woodland consumed like grass, extending to mountains, hills and forests. Both use combustible vegetation to picture devastating judgment, with different plants named.
triples.source_text: For it will be laid waste to their foundation, consumed like an entwining thorn-vine and like stubble full of dryness.

target_units.text: And it will not be so; rather, the Lord Sabaoth will send dishonor against your honor, and against your glory a burning fire will burn.
Israel’s light will become fire, and He will sanctify him in burning fire and consume the woodland like grass. On that day,
the mountains, hills and forests will be extinguished, and it will consume from soul to flesh. The one fleeing will be like someone fleeing from a burning flame.

triples.relationship: same-chapter recurrence of schemes against the Lord
triples.rationale: Nahum 1:11 identifies a scheme devising evil in opposition to the Lord. The earlier question in 1:9 asks what is devised against Him and announces His response. The repeated devising language develops the same accusation within the chapter.
triples.source_text: From you will come a scheme, devising evil things in opposition to the Lord.

target_units.text: What do you devise against the Lord? He will make a complete end; He will not exact vengeance twice upon the same thing in affliction.

triples.relationship: the Lord's authority over many waters
triples.rationale: Nahum introduces the Lord as the One who rules many waters. The psalm likewise places the Lord over many waters and His voice over the waters. The shared description identifies the authority of the speaker, without making the subsequent threats identical.
triples.source_text: Thus says the Lord who rules many waters: Even so they will be separated, and your report will no longer be heard.

target_units.text: The Lord’s voice is over the waters; the God of glory thundered; the Lord is over many waters.

triples.relationship: release from an oppressor's rod and yoke
triples.rationale: Nahum promises to crush his rod away and tear apart bonds. Isaiah tells the people not to fear the Assyrian's rod and promises the removal and destruction of his yoke. Both describe liberation through the removal of instruments of oppression.
triples.source_text: And now I will crush his rod away from you and tear apart your bonds.

target_units.text: Therefore thus says the Lord Sabaoth: “Do not fear the Assyrians, My people dwelling in Zion, because he will strike you with a rod; for I bring a blow upon you to see Egypt’s way.
For yet a little while, and the wrath will cease, but My anger will be against their counsel.”
God will rouse action against them according to Midian’s blow in a place of affliction, and His anger on the way by the sea, toward the way by Egypt.
On that day his fear will be removed from you and his yoke from your shoulder, and the yoke will be destroyed from your shoulders.

triples.relationship: the Lord destroys carved images
triples.rationale: Nahum announces the destruction of carved and cast images from the house of the addressed one's god. Micah likewise announces the Lord's destruction of carved images and pillars and the end of bowing to human handiwork. The shared action concerns images, while the addressed settings differ.
triples.source_text: The Lord will command concerning you: No more will be sown from your name. From the house of your god I will destroy carved and cast images. I will make your burial, for they are swift.

target_units.text: I will destroy your carved images and pillars from your midst, and you will certainly no longer bow down to the works of your hands.

triples.relationship: shared announcement of good news and peace upon the mountains
triples.rationale: Nahum calls attention to the feet on the mountains of one bringing good news and announcing peace. Isaiah likewise combines mountains, feet, good news and a report of peace, alongside salvation and God's reign. The distinctive cluster of images directly connects the announcements.
triples.source_text: Look, upon the mountains are the feet of one bringing good news and announcing peace! Celebrate your feasts, Judah; repay your vows. For they will no longer pass through you into decay. It has been completed; it has been removed.

target_units.text: like beauty on the mountains, like the feet of one proclaiming a report of peace, like one bringing good news. For I will make your salvation heard, saying, ‘Zion, your God will reign.’”

triples.relationship: later scriptural use of the good-news messenger's feet
triples.rationale: Nahum depicts the feet of one bringing good news and peace. Romans introduces written Scripture about the beautiful feet of those announcing good things within its discussion of sent proclaimers. The shared messenger image is retained without claiming Romans names Nahum as its source.
triples.source_text: Look, upon the mountains are the feet of one bringing good news and announcing peace! Celebrate your feasts, Judah; repay your vows. For they will no longer pass through you into decay. It has been completed; it has been removed.

target_units.text: And how are they to proclaim unless they are sent? Just as it is written, “How beautiful are the feet of those announcing good things!”

triples.relationship: the Lord's opposition to Jacob's arrogance
triples.rationale: Nahum says the Lord turned away Jacob's arrogance, alongside Israel's arrogance and their ravaged vine branches. Amos likewise declares the Lord's abhorrence of all Jacob's arrogance before threatening the city. The connection preserves the native arrogance wording rather than substituting restoration of splendor.
triples.source_text: because the Lord turned away Jacob’s arrogance, as Israel’s arrogance; for those shaking them out shook out both them and their vine branches; they ruined

target_units.text: For the Lord swore by Himself: “I abhor all Jacob’s arrogance and have hated his regions; I will remove the city with all who inhabit it.”

triples.relationship: weapons broken within descriptions of destructive power
triples.rationale: Nahum's sentence continues from 2:3 into the ruining of the weapons of might, followed by mighty men playing in fire and troubled horsemen. The psalm explicitly describes the Lord breaking a weapon apart and burning shields. The connection concerns ruined military equipment; it does not make the agents or every fire detail identical.
triples.source_text: the weapons of their might from among people, mighty men playing in fire. The reins of their chariots are on the day of his preparation, and the horsemen will be thrown into uproar

target_units.text: Bringing wars to an end as far as the earth’s limits, He will shatter a bow and break a weapon apart and burn shields in fire.

triples.relationship: chariots and fiery imagery in an advancing force
triples.rationale: Nahum describes chariots in confused motion with an appearance like fire torches and flashing lightning. Joel compares the advancing force to horses and chariots and its sound to a fiery flame. Both combine swift military movement with fire imagery, using distinct descriptions.
triples.source_text: in the roads, and the chariots will be thrown into confusion and entangled in the squares; their appearance is like torches of fire and lightning flashing past.

target_units.text: Their appearance is like the sight of horses; like riders they will pursue.
With a sound like chariots they will leap upon mountain peaks, like the sound of a fiery flame devouring stubble, like a numerous and strong people arrayed for war.

triples.relationship: defensive preparations at city walls
triples.rationale: Nahum describes nobles hurrying to the walls and preparing defenses amid weakness. Isaiah describes Jerusalem's houses pulled down to fortify the wall and water provided between walls. Both depict city defenses being prepared under threat, with different specified preparations.
triples.source_text: Their nobles will remember and flee by day; they will weaken on their journey, hurry to the walls and prepare their defenses.

target_units.text: and uncover the hidden things of the houses in David’s citadel. They saw that they were many and that the old pool’s water had been diverted into the city,
and that Jerusalem’s houses had been pulled down to fortify the city’s wall.
You provided water for yourselves between the two walls, inside the old pool, and did not look to the One who made her from the beginning or see the One who founded her.

triples.relationship: the plundering of a city's accumulated possessions
triples.rationale: Nahum describes silver and gold being plundered amid abundant adornment and desirable vessels. Ezekiel's oracle against Tyre likewise announces the stripping of possessions and demolition of desirable houses. The connection concerns the seizure of urban wealth, without identifying the two cities.
triples.source_text: They were plundering silver; they were plundering gold. There was no limit to her adornment; they have been weighed down beyond all her desirable vessels.

target_units.text: He will plunder your strength, strip your possessions, throw down your walls, and demolish your desirable houses. He will throw your stones, timber, and dust into the sea.

triples.relationship: bodily collapse and burning faces amid terror
triples.rationale: Nahum combines broken hearts, loosening knees, pains at the waist and faces like a scorching pot. Isaiah likewise describes slackened hands, cowardly souls, labor pains and faces changed as to flame. Both gather bodily weakness, pains and fiery facial imagery to describe terror.
triples.source_text: Shaking out, tossing up and boiling over; broken hearts, loosening knees, pangs at every waist, and every face like the scorching of a pot.

target_units.text: Therefore every hand will slacken, and every human soul grow cowardly;
the envoys will be troubled, and labor pains will hold them like those of a woman giving birth. They will lament to one another and be distraught, and change their face as to flame.

triples.relationship: ruling power pictured as lions and cubs
triples.rationale: Nahum asks where the lions' dwelling and cubs' pasture have gone. Ezekiel introduces a lament over Israel's ruler with a mother among lions and her cub becoming a prey-seizing lion. Both present political power through a lion family, in different national settings.
triples.source_text: Where is the lions’ dwelling and the pasture that belonged to the cubs, where a lion went to enter there, a lion’s cub, and no one frightened them?

target_units.text: “And you, take up a lament over Israel’s ruler,
and say: What was your mother? A cub! She came to be among lions; among lions she multiplied her cubs.
One of her cubs sprang away; he became a lion, learned to seize prey, and ate human beings.

triples.relationship: a lion's predation pictures destructive rule
triples.rationale: Nahum's lion fills its nest with prey and dwelling with plunder for its young. Ezekiel likewise depicts a lion learning to seize prey, eating people and desolating cities. Both apply predatory lion behavior to destructive power.
triples.source_text: A lion seized enough for his cubs and strangled for his lions; he filled his nest with prey and his dwelling with plunder.

target_units.text: He moved among lions, became a lion, learned to seize prey, and ate human beings.
He fed in his boldness, desolated their cities, and destroyed the land and its fullness by the sound of his roaring.

triples.relationship: the ending of a lion's power and audible activity
triples.rationale: Nahum announces the destruction of lions and prey, after which the addressed one's deeds will not be heard again. Ezekiel likewise describes nations capturing the lion and imprisoning him so his voice will not be heard on Israel's mountains. The lion image ends in removal in both, with different stated actions silenced.
triples.source_text: Look, I am against you, says the Lord Almighty. I will burn your multitude in smoke; the sword will consume your lions. I will destroy your prey from the earth, and your deeds will never again be heard.

target_units.text: Nations from the surrounding countries set themselves against him and spread their nets over him; he was caught in their destruction.
They put him in a muzzle and a cage. He came to Babylon’s king, and he brought him into prison, so that his voice would not be heard upon Israel’s mountains.

triples.relationship: a city accused of bloodshed and lawlessness
triples.rationale: Nahum addresses a city of bloodshed, falsehood and injustice. Ezekiel likewise commands judgment of the city of bloodshed and displays its lawless deeds, blood and defilement. Both frame the city's coming judgment through an explicit bloodshed accusation.
triples.source_text: O city of bloodshed, wholly false, full of injustice! Prey will not be touched.

target_units.text: “And you, son of man, will you judge the city of bloodshed? Display all her lawless deeds to her,
and say, ‘Thus says the Lord, the Lord: O city shedding blood within her so that her time may come, making reflections against herself to defile herself!

Through their blood that you shed you have transgressed, and through your reflections that you made you were being defiled. You brought your days near and brought the season of your years. Therefore I have made you a reproach to the nations and a mockery to all the countries

triples.relationship: the sound of horses announces a destructive approach
triples.rationale: Nahum describes the sounds of whips, wheels, a pursuing horse and a jolting chariot within the attack scene. Jeremiah likewise makes the sound of horses and their neighing herald an attacker who devours a city and its inhabitants. Both evoke an assault through the sound of its horses.
triples.source_text: The sound of whips and the sound of shaking wheels, of a pursuing horse and a jolting chariot,

target_units.text: From Dan we will hear the shrill sound of his horses; at the sound of the neighing of his riding horses the whole earth shook. And he will come and devour the earth and its fullness, a city and those dwelling in it.

triples.relationship: multitudes of slain in a judgment against nations
triples.rationale: Nahum's mounted attack culminates in a multitude of slain and a grievous fall. Isaiah likewise announces wrath against nations, handing them to slaughter, with wounded and dead thrown out. Both describe mass casualties within judgment upon nations.
triples.source_text: and of a mounting horseman, a flashing sword and glittering weapons, a multitude of slain and a grievous fall! There was no limit to her nations, and they will weaken in their bodies

target_units.text: For the Lord’s wrath is against all nations, and anger against their number, to destroy them and hand them over to slaughter.
Their wounded and dead will be thrown out; their odor will rise, and mountains will be soaked with their blood.

triples.relationship: a powerful city accused of prostitution and sorcery
triples.rationale: Nahum describes the city as a prostitute and mistress of potions, selling nations and tribes through these practices. Isaiah addresses Babylon with accusations of prostitution, sorcery and enchantments before its destruction. Both combine these accusations against a personified city, without equating every alleged action.
triples.source_text: because of the multitude of prostitution. A prostitute, beautiful and pleasing, mistress of potions, selling nations through her prostitution and tribes through her potions,

target_units.text: Now these two will come upon you suddenly, in one day: widowhood and childlessness will come suddenly upon you, amid your sorcery and the overwhelming power of your enchanters,

in your hope of wickedness. For you said, ‘I am, and there is no other.’ Know that understanding these things and your prostitution will become your shame. You said in your heart, ‘I am, and there is no other.’

Destruction will come upon you, and you will certainly not know it—a pit, and you will fall into it. Misery will come upon you, and you will certainly not be able to become clean. Destruction will come upon you suddenly, and you will certainly not know it.
Stand now amid your enchantments and your abundant sorcery, which you learned from youth, if you can be helped.

triples.relationship: a personified city's shame is exposed
triples.rationale: Nahum announces exposed hind parts, shame shown to nations and dishonor to kingdoms. Isaiah likewise commands Babylon to uncover and declares that her shame and reproaches will become visible. Both present public exposure as the humiliation of a city figured as a woman.
triples.source_text: look, I am against you, says the Lord God Almighty. I will expose your hind parts over your face and show nations your shame and kingdoms your dishonor,

target_units.text: Take a millstone and grind flour. Uncover your veil, expose your gray hair, pull up your garments to bare your lower legs, and cross rivers.
Your shame will be uncovered, and your reproaches will be visible. I will exact justice from you; I will certainly no longer hand it over to humans.”

triples.relationship: defilement leads to public disgrace before other peoples
triples.rationale: Nahum announces abomination cast upon the city according to its impurities and its being made an example. Ezekiel likewise links defilement and bloodshed to the city becoming a reproach and mockery among nearby and distant countries. Both describe public disgrace associated with the city's impurities.
triples.source_text: and cast abomination upon you according to your impurities, and make you an example,

target_units.text: Through their blood that you shed you have transgressed, and through your reflections that you made you were being defiled. You brought your days near and brought the season of your years. Therefore I have made you a reproach to the nations and a mockery to all the countries
near you and far away from you. They will mock you: “Unclean, the famous one, abundant in lawless deeds!”

triples.relationship: passersby react to Nineveh's devastation
triples.rationale: Nahum describes everyone seeing miserable Nineveh springing away and questioning who will lament her. Zephaniah likewise names Nineveh's wasteland and describes passersby hissing and waving their hands. Both make onlookers' responses part of the same named city's humiliation.
triples.source_text: and everyone seeing you will spring away and say, “Miserable Nineveh! Who will lament her? Where shall I seek consolation for her?”

target_units.text: He will stretch His hand against the north and destroy the Assyrian, making Nineveh a waterless wasteland like a wilderness.

Flocks and all the wild animals of the earth will graze within her; chameleons and hedgehogs will lie in her recessed panels. Wild animals will cry in her openings, and ravens in her gateways, for cedar is her structure.

This is the contemptuous city dwelling in confidence, saying in her heart, “I am, and there is no one after me.” How she became a wasteland, pasture for wild animals! Everyone passing through her will hiss and wave his hands.

triples.relationship: Egypt, Ethiopia and Libyan support within announced defeat
triples.rationale: Nahum names Ethiopia and Egypt as strength and Libyans as helpers in the account of Amon. Ezekiel likewise groups Egypt, Ethiopia and Libyans in a sword judgment and says Egypt's supports will fall. The named network of support connects the passages without identifying all their cities or events.
triples.source_text: and Ethiopia was her strength, and Egypt, and there is no limit to the flight; Libyans became her helpers.

target_units.text: A sword will come upon the Egyptians, and there will be turmoil in Ethiopia; wounded men will fall in Egypt, and her foundations will collapse together.
Persians, Cretans, Lydians, Libyans, all the mixed company, and some of the sons of My covenant will fall by the sword in her.
Egypt’s supports will fall, and the arrogance of her strength will come down from Migdol to Syene; they will fall in her by the sword, says the Lord.

triples.relationship: infants dashed to the ground amid a city's defeat
triples.rationale: Nahum describes the addressed city's deportation, infants dashed down and nobles bound. Hosea likewise announces Samaria's disappearance, sword deaths and nursing infants dashed to the ground. The particular violence against infants is shared, with different cities named.
triples.source_text: She too will go into deportation as a captive; they will dash her infants to the ground at the head of all her roads, cast lots for all her glorious things; and all her nobles will be bound in handcuffs.

target_units.text: Samaria will disappear because she opposed her God. They will fall by the sword; their nursing infants will be dashed to the ground, and their pregnant women will be ripped open.

triples.relationship: a defeated city portrayed as drunken
triples.rationale: Nahum says the addressed city too will become drunk and seek a place away from enemies. Isaiah describes Jerusalem drunk from the Lord's cup of anger and promises that cup to its oppressors. Both portray a city's affliction through drunkenness, with Isaiah explicitly identifying its cup imagery.
triples.source_text: You too will become drunk and be overlooked; you too will seek a place to stand away from enemies.

target_units.text: Awake, awake, rise, Jerusalem, you who drank the cup of anger from the Lord’s hand. You drank out and emptied the cup of falling, the bowl of anger.
There was no one to comfort you among all your children you bore, and no one to take your hand among all your sons you raised.
These two confront you—who will grieve with you?—fall and crushing, famine and sword. Who will comfort you?
Your sons are helpless, sleeping at every way out like a half-boiled beet, full of the Lord’s anger, exhausted because of the Lord God.
Therefore listen, humbled one, drunk but not from wine.
Thus says the Lord God who judges His people: ‘Behold, I have taken from your hand the cup of falling, the bowl of anger. You will not drink it again.
I will throw it into the hands of those who wronged and humbled you, who told your soul, “Bend down, so we may pass.” You laid your back level with the earth, outside for passersby.’”

triples.relationship: a vulnerable object of judgment compared to a readily eaten fig
triples.rationale: Nahum compares fortresses with fig trees that fall into the eater's mouth if shaken. Isaiah likewise compares fallen glory with an early fig that a viewer wants to swallow immediately. The fig-eating image portrays how readily what seemed substantial can be consumed.
triples.source_text: All your fortresses are fig trees having lookouts; if shaken, they will fall into the eater’s mouth.

target_units.text: The flower fallen from the hope of glory, on the high mountain’s summit, will be like an early fig: whoever sees it will want to swallow it before taking it into his hand.

triples.relationship: defenders compared with women and defensive bars destroyed
triples.rationale: Nahum says the people are like women, the gates open to enemies and fire consumes bars. Jeremiah likewise describes Babylon's crushed warriors becoming like women, dwellings burned and bars shattered. The linked military simile and ruined defenses closely connect the defeat scenes.
triples.source_text: Look, your people within you are like women! The gates of your land will open wide to your enemies, and fire will consume your bars.

target_units.text: Babylon’s warrior has ceased fighting; they will sit there in confinement. Their power was crushed; they became like women. Her dwellings were burned; her bars were shattered.

triples.relationship: water supplies and fortifications prepared for siege
triples.rationale: Nahum commands drawing siege water and holding fortresses while working mud, straw and brick. Isaiah describes water diverted into the city, walls strengthened and water provided between walls. Both describe practical defensive preparations, without assigning identical building materials to the passages.
triples.source_text: Draw water for yourself for the siege, hold your fortresses firmly; step into mud, be trampled in straw, hold fast over the brick.

target_units.text: and uncover the hidden things of the houses in David’s citadel. They saw that they were many and that the old pool’s water had been diverted into the city,
and that Jerusalem’s houses had been pulled down to fortify the city’s wall.
You provided water for yourselves between the two walls, inside the old pool, and did not look to the One who made her from the beginning or see the One who founded her.

triples.relationship: locust devouring used to portray destruction
triples.rationale: Nahum describes fire and sword consuming the city and compares devouring with a locust. Joel names successive caterpillar, locust, bruchus and blight devouring what remains. The shared connection is destructive devouring by locusts; Nahum expressly applies it as a comparison.
triples.source_text: There fire will consume you; a sword will destroy you, devouring you like a locust, and you will become heavy like a crawling locust.

target_units.text: What the caterpillar left, the locust devoured; what the locust left, the bruchus locust devoured; what the bruchus locust left, the blight devoured.

triples.relationship: same-chapter flight represented by locusts
triples.rationale: Nahum 3:16 follows multiplied trading with a crawling locust rushing out and flying away. The next verse likewise depicts a mixed company leaping away like locusts when the sun rises. The repeated insects' departure develops the chapter's image of disappearing strength.
triples.source_text: You multiplied your trading beyond the stars of heaven. A crawling locust rushed out and flew away.

target_units.text: Your mixed company leaped away like a young locust, like a locust perched on a fence on frosty days. The sun rose, it leaped away, and it did not know its place. Woe to them!

triples.relationship: people scattered on mountains without effective shepherds
triples.rationale: Nahum describes slumbering shepherds, rulers put to sleep and people departed upon mountains with no one receiving them. Micaiah likewise sees Israel scattered on mountains like a flock without a shepherd. Both portray the people dispersed without leadership, in different national settings.
triples.source_text: Your shepherds slumbered; the Assyrian king put your rulers to sleep. Your people departed upon the mountains, and there was no one receiving them.

target_units.text: Micaiah said, “Not so! I have seen all Israel scattered on the mountains like a flock without a shepherd. The Lord said, ‘These have no master. Let each return to his own house in peace.’”

triples.relationship: Nineveh's fall draws a hostile public response
triples.rationale: Nahum ends with hearers clapping over the news of the addressed power's incurable wound because of its continual evil. Zephaniah names Nineveh's devastation and passersby hissing and waving hands. Both depict public reaction to the arrogant city's ruin, while Nahum explicitly gives its widespread evil as the reason.
triples.source_text: There is no healing for your crushing; your wound has become inflamed. All who hear the report of you will clap their hands over you, for upon whom has your evil not continually come?

target_units.text: He will stretch His hand against the north and destroy the Assyrian, making Nineveh a waterless wasteland like a wilderness.

Flocks and all the wild animals of the earth will graze within her; chameleons and hedgehogs will lie in her recessed panels. Wild animals will cry in her openings, and ravens in her gateways, for cedar is her structure.

This is the contemptuous city dwelling in confidence, saying in her heart, “I am, and there is no one after me.” How she became a wasteland, pasture for wild animals! Everyone passing through her will hiss and wave his hands.
